Jotham
JOH-thuhm
proper noun (figure)
Hebrew Yotham (H3147) — "Yahweh is perfect/complete" or possibly "the LORD is upright." From Yah (the divine name) + tam ("perfect, complete, blameless").

📖 Biblical Definition

Jotham (c. 750 — 735 BC) was the eleventh king of Judah (2 Kings 15:32-38; 2 Chronicles 27), son of the leprous king Uzziah/Azariah, contemporary of the prophets Isaiah, Hosea, and Micah whose ministries opened during his reign. Sixteen-year reign according to the canonical accession formula. He is one of only four Judahite kings the Chronicler can describe without qualification as having done right in the sight of the LORD (the others being Asa, Hezekiah, and Josiah) — though even this praise is followed by the standard note that the high places were not removed (2 Kings 15:35). His name — "Yahweh is perfect" — was reflected in his personal integrity: "So Jotham became mighty, because he prepared his ways before the LORD his God" (2 Chr 27:6). His public record is light by Chronicler standards: he built the upper gate of the temple, fortified the walls of Ophel, and successfully campaigned against the Ammonites who paid him a hundred talents of silver, ten thousand measures of wheat, and ten thousand of barley for three years running (2 Chr 27:5). The most theologically striking detail is the Chronicler's observation in 2 Chr 27:2: he did right "howbeit he entered not into the temple of the LORD" — a deliberate reverent restraint after his father Uzziah was struck with leprosy for entering the temple to offer incense (2 Chr 26:16-21). Jotham learned the lesson his father had to be struck with leprosy to learn: priestly and kingly offices are distinct and the king does not invade priestly territory. The Isaiah, Hosea, and Micah prophecies dated to Jotham's reign give us his most enduring legacy: under a faithful but quiet king the great writing prophets of the eighth century began the public ministry that would shape Old Testament canon and call Judah toward and beyond the exile.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Eleventh king of Judah (c. 750-735 BC); son of leprous Uzziah; reigned 16 years; one of only four Judahite kings the Chronicler can call wholly faithful (with Asa, Hezekiah, Josiah); contemporary of Isaiah, Hosea, and Micah whose prophetic ministries began under him.

JOTHAM, proper noun. Hebrew Yotham (H3147) — "Yahweh is perfect/complete," from Yah + tam.

Eleventh king of the divided southern kingdom of Judah (c. 750-735 BC); son of the leprous king Uzziah (Azariah); father of the wicked Ahaz.

Reigned 16 years; one of only four Judahite kings called wholly faithful by the Chronicler (with Asa, Hezekiah, Josiah).

Built the upper gate of the temple, fortified the wall of Ophel, subdued the Ammonites; "entered not into the temple of the LORD" out of reverent restraint (2 Chr 27:2).

Contemporary of Isaiah, Hosea, and Micah whose canonical prophetic ministries began during his reign.

📖 Key Scripture

2 Chronicles 27:6 — "So Jotham became mighty, because he prepared his ways before the LORD his God."

2 Chronicles 27:2 — "And he did that which was right in the sight of the LORD, according to all that his father Uzziah did: howbeit he entered not into the temple of the LORD. And the people did yet corruptly."

Isaiah 1:1 — "The vision of Isaiah the son of Amoz, which he saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah."

Micah 1:1 — "The word of the LORD that came to Micah the Morasthite in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Jotham is corrupted when his quiet faithfulness is overlooked in favor of his more dramatic predecessors and successors, when his "entered not into the temple" restraint is treated as a footnote rather than as a deliberate Chronicler-emphasized lesson learned from his father's leprosy, or when the prophets of his reign are read in isolation from the kingly context the Chronicler carefully preserves.

expand to see more

Quiet-king neglect. Sandwiched between his more dramatic father (Uzziah's leprosy) and his more dramatic son (Ahaz's apostasy), Jotham receives only twelve verses of attention in 2 Kings 15:32-38 and a modest chapter in 2 Chronicles 27. Many readers skip him. But the Chronicler signals his importance by giving him the wholly-faithful designation (with Asa, Hezekiah, and Josiah) and the rare unqualified verdict of his strength deriving from his prepared ways. The lesson is doctrinal: quiet faithfulness is not less worthy of canonical attention than dramatic apostasy or reform. The Chronicler models the discipline of seeing it.

Temple-restraint underestimated. 2 Chr 27:2's note that Jotham did right "howbeit he entered not into the temple of the LORD" is rendered in many translations and read by many readers as a passing remark. The Chronicler intended it as a key explanatory contrast with his father: Uzziah had entered the temple to offer incense and was struck with leprosy on the spot (2 Chr 26:16-21). Jotham, watching his father live the last years of his reign in a separate house as a leper, learned the lesson. The restraint is not a footnote; it is a son refusing the office-confusion that destroyed his father.
